article.title: Taare Zameen Par: Celebrities break silence, back CJP-led youth uprising - Alt News

article.full_text: Several celebrities have come out in support of the youth-led protests that have swept Delhi since July 20, condemning the police crackdown on demonstrators and backing the students’ demands for accountability and education reforms. The ‘Sansad Chalo’ march, led by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), drew tens of thousands of protesters demanding the resignation of Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan and comprehensive reforms to India’s education system. The movement grew out of the NEET-UG paper leak and examination cancellation, which allegedly drove at least 20 students to suicide, and gathered further momentum after climate activist Sonam Wangchuk was forcefully removed while on a 20-day hunger strike in solidarity with the students. The protest, however, was met with an unprecedented police crackdown. Police used lathi-charge, tear gas, pellet guns and shock batons against demonstrators, leaving hundreds injured and hospitalised and drawing global condemnation. The public show of solidarity from actors, filmmakers, musicians and other public figures stands out at a time when India’s entertainment industry has often been criticised for remaining silent during moments of political upheaval and national crises. While many of the country’s biggest celebrities have chosen not to comment, several others have publicly backed the youth protesters—some by joining demonstrations in person and others through messages on social media. Among the most prominent and active supporters was actor Shabana Azmi. Joining the protest on July 19, a day prior to the march, she met CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke and extended support to the students on hunger strike. She lauded the fasting students’ bravery and thanked Wangchuk for his leadership. “The spark which has been lit will not go out. Even if you put these protesters in jail today, you cannot keep them in jail forever. This spark has now flared up and will turn into a roaring flame,” she had said. Azmi was also tear gassed along with the other protesters and appeared seemingly ill; however, she kept posting updates of the protest via her Instagram page. Sharing a video while being bundled up inside a truck with other protesters, she shared a couplet by her father and acclaimed poet, Kaifi Azmi, exalting the students’ courage. Alongside Azmi in the truck was actor, film director, and activist Prakash Raj. A vocal critic of the ruling party, Raj had met a fasting Wangchuk on July 11. “In solidarity with the youngsters of my country at #JantarMantar,” he wrote on his Instagram page while sharing photos from the hunger strike. He reached Jantar Mantar on July 19, spent the night with the demonstrators and joined the ‘Chalo Sansad’ march the next day. He posted multiple updates from the protest, extending full solidarity with the demonstrators and displaying the extent of police clampdown. Asked about the silence of a majority of Bollywood stars on issues plaguing the country, Raj told Peek TV from the protest site, “People who speak, the world is watching…who will stand by the people. Simple…Now you know who is what. Such movements show who has got the integrity, who will stand for the people. Who am I to say? I can talk to myself. People have great voices, great actors…I wish they used it for this. They have not, people will judge. When history will be written tomorrow, they may forgive who might have made the mistake but they will never forgive who was silent.” Another actor who physically joined the stir on July 20 was Amol Parashar. “I cried myself to sleep last night,” he wrote in a heartfelt note on his Instagram page, recalling his experience of the protest turning violent as police began cracking down on the peaceful protesters. Explaining that he quietly joined the protest without informing anyone because he was deeply moved by the students’ messages to him asking him to join the protest, he condemned the police attacks. “The state decided that it had had enough of these foreign influenced children and decided to break their heads, so these ideas could escape from the hole in their skull. Young people bleeding on the road, their friends crying for help. Some just shocked and in disbelief, asking the cops “hum aapke bacche nahi hain kya?”. They came asking for better education, they left with a harsh lesson: no one cares about you,” he wrote in his post. While a fake video purporting actor Naseeruddin Shah’s presence at the Jantar Mantar protest, along with his two sons, Vivaan and Imaad Shah, was being widely circulated on social media, Shah took to Instagram on July 22, voicing his support for the students and condemning the police brutality. ALSO READ: Old video from Mumbai falsely circulated as Naseeruddin Shah joining Jantar Mantar stir In a video statement, a staunch critic of the ruling dispensation, the actor said (translated from Hindi), “If an uneducated person runs this country, his heart will want that the entire country becomes uneducated, foolish, incompetent, and merciless like him. Right now, my heart is aching and I am also boiling with anger watching how our kids have been treated by these goons who remind me of American ICE agents, wearing masks and carrying sticks…Think about your own children sometimes and think that you will get your due one day for sure…” Singer Arijit Singh, who seldom speaks up on social issues and is widely known to remain off the grid, strongly criticised the police brutality via his private account. Subsequently, a user commented on Singh’s post that he has now lost all respect for the artist. Singh responded assertively, “I am not worried about the fact that somebody respects me or not. I am also not bothered about anyone’s opinion as everyone have their own. you being a fan of me doesn’t compel me to say sugarcoated words to you. but I apologise to you as a person…It’s just that I am angry. Forgive me to become free. You can delete all my playlist and forget my existence. be happy I genuinely pray for your happiness. but that doesn’t change my opinion.” One of the first and few mainstream Bollywood celebrities to speak out in support of Wangchuk, Sonakshi Sinha lauded his hunger strike in support of the students’ cause. “I cannot stay silent anymore…now whatever has to happen, will happen,” she had said in a video posted on her Instagram page on July 16, while demanding answers from the government. “Why is nobody listening? Nobody cares. Nobody is open for a dialogue…I am not an anti-national, I am a citizen of this country.” Later on July 18, Sinha posted another video criticising the forceful removal of Wangchuk from the protest site to Safdarjung Hospital. “What happened with Sonam sir today wasn’t right…No matter what has been going on, they have stayed calm, respectful, and have kept their point forward without violence. We all know the country’s strength is in its youth…Even after all the discomfort, disappointment and difficulties, the way you have held on to your beliefs, hats off to you.” Sharing visuals of the protest, she condemned the police action. She wrote: “20th July…bohot logon ki haddiyaan tooti aur ek POORE DESH ka dil toota. Yaad rakhna” (20th July…many people suffered broken bones, and an entire nation’s heart was broken. Remember that.) Shreya Dhanwanthary: ‘Being Brave Now Is The Most Obvious Choice’ Similarly sharing visuals of the youth demonstrators being lathi-charged by Delhi police, film and TV actor Shreya Dhanwanthary wrote on Instagram: “Fight. If you can’t fight, speak up. If you can’t speak up, write. If you can’t write, support. If you can’t support, give company. If you can’t give company, boost morale. If you can’t do anything then atleast don’t stand in the way of those who do.” The following day, she posted another video on the burden of the speaking up on social issues as a public figure. She said her determination to speak up against injustices has cost her many opportunities and attracted hate, while highlighting how much speaking up matters. “It matters that you are standing on the right side of history…even if you are not present physically or going there and facing police brutality and facing violence at the hands of the those who were sworn to protect you. The government is not India, the ruling party is not India…India is made up you and I and everybody else that is fighting…Being brave now is the most obvious choice,” she said. Bollywood actor Dia Mirza took to Instagram Stories to condemn the police brutality on July 20. “Today has been a day that has revealed many truths. A day thousands of people showed up to mark their protest demanding accountability, transparency and reform for the education system…A day when the forces that are duty bound to protect it’s citizens used brute force on them including women and children in reaction to their peaceful protest. Hopeful and angry,” she wrote. Further, Mirza expressed disappointment over Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s July 23 statement. She highlighted that his statement came 47 days after the protests and hunger strikes began, adding that even now he has said “nothing”. “Nothing can heal the millions of hearts that are broken.” Echoing his peers’ disappointment over the police brutality, filmmaker and vocal critic of societal injustices, Anurag Kashyap on July 2o wrote on his Instagram post (translated from Hindi), “I never knew that wearing the uniform demanded a bargain with one’s soul, humanity, and conscience. Is there not a single police officer in this country who can stand up and say, ‘I will not obey this order because it is wrong’?” The following day, he posted an image of one Honey Singh Dagar, alleging that he was one of the “plain clothes goons” who beat up students, urging audiences to “identify each one of them”. On the same day, he wrote another post stating that the “kids who have come down to the streets” have only seen “Congress-mukt Bharat and they’re tired of it…They want answers.” Usually known for charity work, another mainstream Bollywood actor who has rarely spoken up on socio-political issues in public, Sonu Sood lent his voice to condemn the police crackdown. “Our students don’t need lathis, they need hands that hug them,” he wrote on his Instagram story. Two Indian men’s national team footballers, Sahal Abdul Samad and Lallianzuala Chhangte, while the former denounced police action against the peaceful protesters, the latter voiced his support for the students’ movement. Actors Soha Ali Khan, Vijay Varma, Riteish Deshmukh and Genelia D’Souza, Ishaan Khatter, and several others chimed in through their social media handles to extend solidarity to the protesting youth and students. Besides the celebrities who showed up Jantar Mantar and those who voiced their support through social media posts, several entertainers joined the CJP solidarity protest at Mumbai’s Shivaji Park on July 22, which saw over 2,000 protesters, including Imran Khan, Huma Qureshi and her brother Saqib Saleem, Ayesha Khan (who was detained by Mumbai police at Worli station), comedians Raunaq Rajani and Abish Mathew (both of whom were detained at Kalachowki station), Gurfateh Pirzada, Akasa Singh and Pratibha Ranta. story.title: The Helmet Stays On
story.skipLabel: Skip this story about celebrities backing the CJP-led youth protests

creativeDirection.dramaticPremise: A young actor must choose between protecting a career opportunity and joining public solidarity after celebrities speak out against the crackdown on student protesters.

dramaticSpine.characterGoal: Mira wants to reach the Mumbai solidarity protest at Shivaji Park before it disperses.
dramaticSpine.obstacle: Kabir insists she protect her audition and avoid possible detention or police violence.
dramaticSpine.newsCatalyst: The article reports that entertainers joined the CJP solidarity protest, while Ayesha Khan, Raunaq Rajani and Abish Mathew were detained at Mumbai stations.
dramaticSpine.reversal: Instead of making Mira retreat, the documented risk exposes how serious the choice has become and makes her willing to lose the audition.
dramaticSpine.costOfFailure: Mira may lose the audition and place herself in danger by attending.
dramaticSpine.emotionalTurn: Kabir stops treating her choice as reckless attention-seeking and recognises that silence is also a choice.
dramaticSpine.resolution: Mira leaves for the protest while Kabir gives her his helmet and follows, accepting the personal risk without pretending it is safe.

visualBible.setting: A cramped Mumbai apartment stairwell opening onto a rain-dark street, moments before the characters leave for Shivaji Park.
visualBible.colorAndLighting: Monsoon blue shadows, warm yellow stairwell bulbs, red reflections from passing traffic, and a gradual shift toward hopeful amber near the exit.
recurringProps: two raincoats hanging on the stair rail
visualBible.storyArc: The stairwell begins as a place of hesitation and becomes a narrow launch point into public action; the helmet passes from fearful protector to shared commitment.
visualBible.referenceImagePrompt: Editorial animated-film still of two fictional young Indian adults together in a cramped Mumbai apartment stairwell: Mira, determined in a teal raincoat with a canvas tote and folded audition slip, and Kabir, anxious in a mustard rain jacket holding a battered yellow scooter helmet. Monsoon rain outside, warm stairwell bulb, blue shadows, red street reflections, cinematic expressive faces, no text, logos, or watermark.

cast.role: Aspiring actor deciding whether to attend the solidarity protest
cast.voiceProfile: Young woman, warm but tightly controlled texture, quick intimate pace; begins defensive and breathless, shifts into steady courage by the final line, with clipped pauses when fear catches up.
cast.visualIdentity: Teal raincoat, short rain-damp hair, canvas tote, folded audition slip tucked into her sleeve.

cast.role: Mira's cousin and practical flatmate, worried about her safety and career
cast.voiceProfile: Young man with a dry, nervous warmth, measured pace and half-swallowed jokes; begins protective and sceptical, turns quietly supportive, ending with a relieved exhale rather than a speech.
cast.visualIdentity: Mustard rain jacket, scuffed trainers, battered yellow scooter helmet, keys clenched in one hand.

beats.dramaticAction: Mira jams her audition slip into her sleeve and reaches for the stairwell door as Kabir blocks it with the helmet.
beats.turningPoint: The named celebrity support makes her departure an immediate personal decision rather than a vague political discussion.

visual.caption: Taare Zameen Par: celebrities back the youth-led protests
visual.imagePrompt: Editorial animated-film close two-shot: Mira shoves a folded audition slip into her teal raincoat sleeve while Kabir blocks the Mumbai stairwell door with a battered yellow helmet; rain beyond the doorway, warm bulb against blue monsoon shadows, anxious comic tension, recurring tote and mustard jacket visible, clean upper-third space for caption, no text, logos, or watermark
visual.scenePrompt: Continuous scene begins in the apartment stairwell as Mira tries to leave and Kabir physically slows her down.
visual.continuityNotes: Establish Mira's teal raincoat, tote, audition slip, Kabir's mustard jacket and yellow helmet; the door remains closed at the end.

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: तारे ज़मीन पर—सेलेब्रिटीज़ चुप्पी तोड़कर CJP की अगुवाई में हो रहे युवा प्रदर्शनों का समर्थन कर रहे हैं। मुझे जाना है।

beats.dramaticAction: Mira pulls the door open; Kabir catches the tote strap and yanks it back before she can step into the rain.
beats.turningPoint: Their harmless argument becomes a physical tug-of-war between career safety and public solidarity.

visual.caption: The choice is no longer comfortable
visual.imagePrompt: Animated cinematic medium shot in the same Mumbai stairwell: Mira lunges through the open door while Kabir catches her canvas tote strap, both off-balance, rain streaks and scooter lights outside, warm bulb overhead, urgent but intimate mood, audition slip peeking from sleeve, upper-third caption-safe space, no text, logos, or watermark
visual.scenePrompt: The door opens onto rain; Kabir stops Mira without hurting her, turning the threshold into the obstacle.
visual.continuityNotes: Keep the door open, tote stretched between them, helmet in Kabir's free hand, and the rain-lit street visible.

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: छात्रों को पीटा गया, उन पर आँसू गैस छोड़ी गई, उन्हें अस्पताल पहुँचाया गया। मैं आज रात टूथपेस्ट वाली मुस्कान के लिए पोज़ नहीं दे सकता।

lines.speaker: kabir
lines.text: और अगर उन्होंने तुम्हें हिरासत में ले लिया तो? तुम्हारा ऑडिशन गया।

beats.dramaticAction: Kabir releases the tote and thrusts his phone toward Mira; she reads, then lowers it instead of retreating.
beats.turningPoint: Reports that Ayesha Khan, Raunaq Rajani and Abish Mathew were detained at Mumbai stations make the danger concrete, but Mira's plan hardens.

visual.caption: Mumbai entertainers joined; some were detained
visual.imagePrompt: Editorial animated-film over-shoulder shot: Kabir thrusts a glowing phone toward Mira in the same stairwell, her face reflected in the screen as she lowers it with sudden resolve; rain, yellow helmet, teal and mustard raincoats, tense blue-and-amber lighting, upper-third space, no readable text, logos, or watermark
visual.scenePrompt: Kabir shows the report as evidence of risk; Mira's hand lowers the phone and reaches for the door latch.
visual.continuityNotes: Preserve the open doorway and stretched tote from the previous shot; phone is a prop for discovery, not a displayed information board.

lines.speaker: kabir
lines.text: आयशा ख़ान को हिरासत में लिया गया। रौनक राजानी और अबिश मैथ्यू को भी—थानों में।

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: तो यह कोई मासूम पोस्ट नहीं है। इसी वजह से मेरा वहाँ पहुँचना ज़रूरी है।

beats.dramaticAction: Mira tears the audition slip in half; Kabir flinches, then takes off his helmet and offers it to her.
beats.turningPoint: Mira pays the immediate career cost, while Kabir's protective gesture changes from resistance to solidarity.

visual.caption: Silence has a cost too
visual.imagePrompt: Animated-film close-up: Mira tears her folded audition slip in two beside the stair rail; Kabir visibly flinches, then removes the battered yellow helmet and offers it across the frame, amber bulb catching the paper edges, emotional monsoon darkness behind, recurring props clear, upper-third caption-safe space, no text, logos, or watermark
visual.scenePrompt: Mira makes the irreversible choice; Kabir responds silently before placing safety equipment in her hands.
visual.continuityNotes: The phone is now lowered and out of focus; maintain the same doorway, rain, tote, and clothing while advancing the torn slip and offered helmet.

lines.speaker: kabir
lines.text: तुमने तो अपना ऑडिशन फाड़कर रख दिया।

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: वे शिक्षा और जवाबदेही की माँग कर रहे हैं। मैं उन्हें अकेले बहादुर बनने के लिए नहीं कह रहा।

beats.dramaticAction: Kabir puts the helmet on Mira, grabs his own raincoat, and locks the apartment behind them as they run downstairs.
beats.turningPoint: He commits to accompanying her, converting fear into a shared, careful choice without claiming the protest is safe.

visual.caption: They leave fear behind—but not caution
visual.imagePrompt: Editorial animated-film wide shot: Kabir fastens the battered yellow helmet on Mira, then locks the apartment door as both run down the rain-slick Mumbai stairwell toward amber streetlight; teal and mustard raincoats, canvas tote, torn paper in Mira's hand, hopeful tense mood, generous upper-third space, no text, logos, or watermark
visual.scenePrompt: The continuous scene ends with both characters leaving the stairwell together for Shivaji Park, moving quickly but not triumphantly.
visual.continuityNotes: Helmet is now on Mira, Kabir carries the tote strap briefly, torn audition slip remains in her hand, and the apartment door closes behind them.

lines.speaker: kabir
lines.text: ठीक है। मैं भी आऊँगा। लेकिन हम साथ रहेंगे—और निकास के पास।

lines.speaker: mira
lines.text: पक्का। हिम्मत पहले। हेलमेट भी पहले।

story.exit: The stairwell door clicks shut behind them; rain swallows the torn audition paper as their footsteps race toward the street.
